summary.text: A 47 year-old female presented to an outpatient wound clinic after self-referral for a second opinion about a full-thickness diabetic foot ulcer of the left plantar mid-foot with a five-plus year history. She had Type 1 diabetes mellitus for 41 years, left eye blindness due to diabetic retinopathy, hypothyroidism and hypertension. Previous interventions included reconstructive surgery for Charcot foot deformity six years previously and, reportedly, total contact casting that was discontinued because she felt unsteady.

Examination and testing showed bilateral Charcot foot deformity, absent protective sensation, a wound measuring 13 × 9 mm with 7 mm depth and a base of 100% slough without clinical signs of infection, 2+ bilateral lower extremity edema and an initial BWAT score of 40. The physical therapy diagnosis was full-thickness diabetic foot ulcer, Wagner grade 1, with a long term goal of complete epithelialization within 16 weeks.

Because the wound had been present for greater than 6 months, MRI and x-ray were obtained and were inconclusive but suggestive of possible osteomyelitis. A tagged WBC scan was negative, and ruling out osteomyelitis was described as accomplished through MRI, tagged WBC scanning and clinical presentation. TCC was not used because she felt unsteady with it in the past and did not want it, and she continued with a walker boot and wheelchair for offloading.

Treatment included sharp and ultrasound debridement, silver hydrofiber dressings, an elastic tubular bandage followed by a three-layer compression wrap, negative pressure wound therapy started at week 4 and discontinued at week eight, adhesive-backed felt offloading from week seven, and a bi-layered living skin equivalent applied at week eight and re-applied at week 12.

At week 15 the wound was 100% epithelialized and closed, the BWAT score had decreased from 40 to 15, and she transitioned into custom molded diabetic footwear. The wound remained closed at the week 16 follow-up visit and all short and long term goals were met, although the author describes a longer than average healing rate.
